newsitem.title: FINLAND: Rautaruukki sees steel prices up in Q3-Q4.
newsitem.headline: Rautaruukki sees steel prices up in Q3-Q4.

text.p: Finnish steel group Rautaruukki Oy sees steel prices continuing to rise this year, though most of the improvement will come in the third or fourth quarter, the group's CEO told a news conference on Monday.

"There is optimism about market conditions in a situation where (steel) prices have begun to rise and are expected to continue to rise, though the increase will be weighted towards the third and fourth quarter," CEO Mikko Kivimaki said.
Prices had already begun to rise "quite significantly" in the second quarter, he said.
Kivimaki was speaking after the group said the state would cut its holding in Rautaruukki to as low as 40 percent from 68.7 percent now in an offering to institutions and retail investors.
Altogether 32.1 million shares, including 13 million new K-series shares, would be offered to domestic and foreign investors, the company said earlier.
"On the whole, we think this year could turn out to be quite a nice one," Kivimaki said, but did not specify how.
Improving prices, economic growth in Europe, normalising stocks and an upswing in construction activity in Finland, Denmark and the new market economies of the Baltic Sea region would help, he said.
Corporate restructuring in the European steel industry, such as a link between Germany's Thyssen and Krupp, would help improve the market situation, Kivimaki said.
"We are trying to gradually achieve a higher and higher level of added value, and to focus on our main markets, in the Baltic Sea region and the nearby areas," Kivimaki said.
"Our labour productivity has risen 30 percent in the 1990s, and will rise by a further 25 percent by the end of the decade," he said.
"In terms of energy consumption we are undoutedly one of the most efficient manufacturers in Europe," Kivimaki said.
Minister of Trade and Industry Antti Kalliomaki told the news conference that the state believed Rautaruukki's shares would prove interesting to domestic as well as foreign investors.
Asked how much the state would bring in from the share sale, he said "About a billion markka... if the sale goes well."

Commenting on the government's plan to retain 40 percent of Rautaruukki, Kalliomaki said parliament had authorised the state to cut its stake to one third, but that it did not necessarily make sense to go all the way to the limit.

He said the state aimed to broaden the company's ownership base: "A broad group of owners will ensure sufficient trade in the stock and improve the chances for efficient price formation on the bourse, and therefore will also benefit existing shareholders."
"I include this (Rautaruukki share sale) in the category that I prefer to call broadening of ownership rather than privatisation," Kalliomaki said.
